tables.caption: Calibration and validation (block B1). Six institutions on two substrates with perfect information, no shock and no lag. $x/\bar x$ is realised gross output relative to the base year; a correct implementation returns 1.000 for every institution, so any departure, any positive shortage rate or any balance residual above $10^{-8}$ is an implementation failure rather than a result.

The information rent of a coordination institution (block B1b): no capacity shock, no reporting lag, only measurement noise ($\sigma=0.03$) and AR(1) demand noise (ar1 $=0.3$, $\sigma=0.02$). Since every institution reproduces the base year exactly when information is perfect (Table~\ref{tab:validation}), any departure here is attributable to the institution's use of information.

Delay and institution (block B2, reference gain 0.30, price elasticity 0.4): the reporting lag $\ell$ is what the scenario sets, the effective delay $k=\ell+1$ is what the theory's $g^*(k)$ refers to, because the planner observes period $t-1-\ell$ when planning $t$. All cells share the same exogenous path (common random numbers), so row differences are institutional, not stochastic.

The gain axis (block B2, extended by Amendment 3). By Amendment 1 the stability test is the price loop of \texttt{tatonnement} (\texttt{price\_gain}, $\varepsilon>0$); the plan-revision loop of \texttt{material\_balance} (\texttt{revision\_gain}) has the opposite sign and is reported as H1$'$.

Sectoral propagation (block B3): a 50 per cent capacity cut lasting eight quarters, one shocked sector at a time, 20 seeds each. $\mathrm{Amp}^{\mathrm{out}}$ is the peak aggregate output loss divided by the output-weighted capacity loss (the like-for-like amplification of H4); the distributional ratio divides the peak *shortage* share by the same denominator and is always larger because it compares a demand-side with a supply-side share.

Incidence of the shortfall (block B3): the engine serves intermediate inputs before final claims, so rationing incidence and production incidence must be read separately. Within the rationed (final) claims, the ``household share'' is the part borne by households and ``gov/invest share'' the part borne by collective and investment demand; intermediate users bear **zero** rationed shortfall by construction and instead bear a plan gap, reported as the rate at which planned intermediate inputs were not supplied.
Administrative rationing against shadow-price coordination (block B4) at three capacity-loss sizes, all with the same eight-quarter duration and the same shocked sector.

The dual-track frontier (block B5): welfare, shortage and price volatility against the plan share $\theta$ at reporting lags 0 and 3. $\theta=0$ is the pure market pole and $\theta=1$ the pure plan pole.

Robustness of the reference condition (block B6): substrate, revision gain, demand and measurement noise, planning effort (internal balance rounds), a 5 per cent perturbation of the input-output matrix, the normative penalty weights at $\pm50$ per cent, and the **labour-slack axis** (rows ``labour*''), which re-runs the B8 decomposition at 1.05--2.00 times labour supply: with little slack the taut plan cannot be executed and costs output, with a lot of slack it can, which turns the second conclusion into a conditional result.

Decomposing material balance (block B8): the proportional revision gain against the number of internal balancing rounds, in the noise-only environment (no shock, no lag, $\sigma_{\mathrm{obs}}=0.03$, AR(1) demand noise). Neither mechanism alone costs output; the loss is in the interaction. The last four columns show the mechanism: balancing is a **downward-only filter** on the plan (``lowered'' counts the quarters in which at least one target came out of the planning step below where it went in), and because investment is a low-priority claimant it absorbs the shortfall (``investment/\bar x falls'), so the capital stock decays and the transitory information error becomes a permanent output loss. Spoilage is output that can be neither used nor stored, bounded by ``max_stock_ratio``.

The local gain of the price loop, measured sector by sector (block B7): $b_{p,j}=-\mathrm{d}s_j/\mathrm{d}\log p_j$ from a $\pm5$ per cent permanent price offset on each good, with that good's capacity permanently cut by 50 per cent and the price gain switched off. The loop gain of the mechanism is $g=\eta\,b_p$, so these numbers decide whether the analytic bound $g^*(m)=2\sin(\pi/(2(2m+1)))$ is reachable at all.

The priority ladder as a treatment (block B2L, exploratory): what happens when essential consumption outranks intermediate inputs under a supply shock. The production-first ladder is the default; the consumption-first ladder is the classic mobilisation-economy alternative.

Where the analytic stability boundary lies, and whether the price loop can reach it (H1). The bound is $g^*(m)=2\sin(\pi/(2(2m+1)))$ on the loop gain $g=\eta\,b_p$; the local gain $b_p$ is measured sector by sector in block B7 (table~\ref{tab:bp_sector}). ``$g_{\max}$'' is the largest loop gain the tested gain grid can produce, $\eta_{\max}b_p$, so ``$g_{\max}/g^*$'' below one means the boundary is **not approachable** in this economy at any adjustment speed inside the grid, whatever its position.
Pre-registered hypotheses and the evidence on them. Every row traces to a test in \texttt{results/tables/tests.csv}; p-values are Holm-corrected within block.
